reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A fluid-filled solitary cavity that most often affects the proximal humerus and proximal femur in children and adolescents
Frequently asymptomatic and discovered incidentally or only after presenting with a pathological fracture
Radiographs show a centrally located, well-defined lucent lesion that does not expand beyond the width of the physis and thins the cortex
The fallen-fragment sign, a bone fragment settling into the dependent part of the fluid-filled cavity after fracture, is characteristic and confirms the lesion is hollow
Distinguished from aneurysmal bone cyst by its central position, single unilocular cavity and clear rather than blood-filled contents
Many lesions resolve or ossify with skeletal maturity, so observation is reasonable for asymptomatic cysts at low fracture risk
Treatment options for at-risk or symptomatic lesions include aspiration and injection, decompression, or curettage with bone grafting
reference.pathophysiology: Unicameral bone cyst is a benign, likely non-neoplastic, fluid-filled cavity of bone lined by a thin fibrous membrane. Its origin is debated but is thought to involve a local disturbance of interstitial fluid drainage and venous outflow within the metaphysis, producing raised intracystic pressure that promotes bone resorption and cavity expansion. Active lesions abut the physis and tend to enlarge, whereas latent lesions migrate away from the growth plate with maturity and often ossify. Cortical thinning predisposes to pathological fracture, which is a common presenting event.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiography to assess location, cortical thinning and proximity to the physis
Recognition of the fallen-fragment sign on radiographs when a fracture is present
MRI or CT to confirm the fluid content and exclude aggressive features when imaging is atypical
Assessment of fracture risk based on cyst size and cortical involvement
Biopsy or aspiration in atypical lesions to confirm the diagnosis and exclude a mimic
redFlags: Aggressive or permeative margins that are atypical for a simple cyst
Impending or established pathological fracture in a weight-bearing bone
Rapid enlargement or an associated soft-tissue mass
Atypical location outside the usual metaphyseal long-bone sites
reference.prognosis: The lesion is benign and often self-limiting, with many cysts healing spontaneously as the skeleton matures. Recurrence after minimally invasive treatment is not uncommon, and repeat procedures are sometimes required before durable healing.
pitfalls: Confusing a simple bone cyst with an aneurysmal bone cyst, which is eccentric and blood-filled
Overtreating an asymptomatic latent cyst that would resolve with growth
Failing to appreciate fracture risk in a large cyst of a weight-bearing bone
Attributing all fluid-filled cystic lesions to a simple cyst without considering aggressive mimics
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Observation with periodic radiographic follow-up for asymptomatic cysts at low fracture risk, since many heal or ossify with skeletal maturity
Minimally invasive intralesional treatment such as corticosteroid injection, autologous bone marrow aspirate injection, or cyst decompression for symptomatic or enlarging lesions
Fracture management, often allowing pathological fractures to unite before or alongside definitive cyst treatment
Curettage and bone grafting for lesions refractory to less invasive measures or at high risk of recurrent fracture
Assessment of fracture risk based on cyst size, cortical thinning and proximity to the physis to guide intervention
Referral to orthopaedic oncology, with biopsy or aspiration of atypical lesions to confirm the diagnosis and exclude a mimic
